Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Great Falls MT
607 PM MST Wed Nov 4 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

 - Generally milder and drier conditions prevail for much of the workweek,
   but a weak front will bring slightly cooler temperatures on 
   Wednesday.

 - Patchy fog development will increase over the next several nights
   over the plains and southwest valleys.

 - Breezy to windy conditions develop over the plains of Central
   and North Central Montana to end the work week and through the
   weekend, especially along the Rocky Mountain Front.

&&

.DISCUSSION...

- Meteorological Overview:

Ridging aloft will shift east of the Northern Rockies to over the
High Plains through Thursday as a shortwave trough over the Gulf 
of Alaska (this afternoon) slides east and over Western Canada and
the Pacific Northwest (Thursday morning).

The aforementioned shortwave trough will bring increasing westerly
winds and spotty mountain precipitation on Thursday as it moves 
over the Northern Rockies from the afternoon through evening 
hours. This trough passage will then usher in an extended period 
of strong westerly flow aloft that will persist into early next 
week despite dominant ridging building for the first half of the 
weekend. The trend of the strongest winds aloft staying north of 
the Canadian border on Friday continues to gain traction, but a 
tightening surface pressure gradient and mountain wave activity 
still looks to enhance stronger winds along the Rocky Mountain 
Front Friday into early Saturday.

Ensembles are favoring the ridge flattening and sending a fast
moving trough into the forecast area Sunday into Monday. This 
will bring another round of winds, strongest along the Rocky 
Mountain Front, and some more light precipitation along the 
northern divide. Temperatures look to remain above average this 
weekend into early next week, with only a slight cool down 
following any shortwave passages. - RCG/Moldan

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

High Winds from Friday through Sunday

Overall confidence in high winds materializing along and west of 
the Interstate 15 corridor to the Continental Divide across 
portions of Central and North Central Montana remains low. ECMWF 
EFIs continue to remain on the low end and below 0.6, which 
considering that November is typically when high wind events 
become more prevalent indicates a borderline event at best. In 
addition to the ECMWF EFIs the NAEFS with respect to cross barrier
flow at H700 indicates wind speeds that are generally only up to 
1 standard deviation above normal. This again would suggest the 
threat for a marginal high wind event. 

While the pressure gradient will be strong at times, approaching 
0.2mb/km across western portions of Glacier County, the that fact 
BUFKIT soundings depict veering winds with height to out of the 
northwest within the critical layer raises concerns about how much
momentum will actually be transferred to the surface, especially 
from Friday through Saturday outside of mountain wave activity. 
For now we will continue to hold off on issuing a High Wind Watch 
given the lack of support for high winds outside of the more 
bullish GEFS members.

.AVIATION...
05/06Z TAF Period

The forecast region and most terminals will have prevailing VFR 
conditions with light winds through tonight with the exception of 
KWYS and KHVR. LIFR with temporary VLIFR due to freezing fog and low 
stratus is expected to develop tonight at and in the areas of KWYS 
with LIFR conditions from freezing fog at KHVR until late morning. 
Scattered low status at KEKS is possible in the morning as well. 
Gustier winds up to 25 KT out of the southwest will develop across 
Central and North Central MT tomorrow by early afternoon with the 
strongest winds of up to 35 KT along the eastern slopes of the Rocky 
Mtn Front and will continue to increase beyond this TAF period. 
Primary hazards will be visibility restrictions from freezing fog 
and mist, mountain obscurations, and potential ice accretion in 
freezing fog. - Akins
